title: Chapter 107 — The Carpenter
paragraphs: Seat yourself like a sultan among the moons of Saturn and take high, abstract man alone; and he seems a wonder, a grandeur, and a woe. But from the same point, take mankind in mass, and for the most part they seem a mob of unnecessary duplicates, both contemporary and hereditary. But humble as he was, and far from furnishing an example of the high, humane abstraction, the Pequod's carpenter was no duplicate. Hence he now comes in person on this stage.

Like all sea-going ship's carpenters, and especially those on whaling vessels, he was, to a certain offhand, practical extent, experienced in many trades and callings alongside his own, the carpenter's trade being the ancient, branching trunk of all those many handicrafts that have more or less to do with wood as a supporting material. But beyond this general remark, which applies to him as well, this carpenter of the Pequod was singularly capable in the thousand nameless mechanical emergencies that keep arising in a large ship on a three- or four-year voyage in uncivilized, far-distant seas. For not to speak of his readiness in ordinary duties — repairing stove boats and sprung spars, reshaping clumsy-bladed oars, setting bull's-eyes (thick glass deck-lights) into the deck or new tree-nails into the side planks, and other miscellaneous matters more directly belonging to his special business — he was also unhesitatingly expert in all sorts of conflicting abilities, both useful and whimsical.

The one grand stage where he performed all his manifold roles was his vice-bench: a long, crude, heavy table furnished with several vises of different sizes, both of iron and of wood. At all times except when whales were alongside, this bench was securely lashed crosswise against the rear of the try-works.

A belaying pin turns out to be too large to go easily into its hole: the carpenter claps it into one of his ever-ready vises and at once files it smaller. A lost land-bird of strange plumage strays on board and is made a captive: out of clean-shaved rods of right-whale bone and crossbeams of sperm whale ivory, the carpenter makes a pagoda-looking cage for it. An oarsman sprains his wrist: the carpenter concocts a soothing lotion. Stubb longed for vermilion stars to be painted on the blade of every one of his oars: screwing each oar into his big wooden vise, the carpenter symmetrically supplies the constellation. A sailor takes a fancy to wear shark-bone earrings: the carpenter drills his ears. Another has a toothache: the carpenter whips out his pincers and, slapping one hand on his bench, tells him to sit there; but the poor fellow flinches uncontrollably before the operation is done; so, whirling round the handle of his wooden vise, the carpenter signals him to clamp his jaw in that, if he wants the tooth drawn.

So this carpenter was prepared at all points, and equally indifferent and without respect in all. Teeth he counted as bits of ivory; heads he regarded as nothing but top-blocks; men themselves he lightly took for capstans. Now, being so variously accomplished over so wide a field, and with such lively expertness too, all this would seem to argue some uncommon quickness of intelligence. But not exactly. For this man was remarkable above all for a certain impersonal stolidity, as it were — impersonal, I say, because it so shaded off into the surrounding infinity of things that it seemed one with the general stolidity visible in the whole world, which, while ceaselessly active in countless ways, still eternally holds its peace and ignores you, though you dig foundations for cathedrals. Yet this half-horrible stolidity in him, which seemed to involve an all-branching heartlessness too, was oddly mixed at times with an old, crutch-like, antediluvian, wheezing humor, streaked now and then with a certain grizzled wit, such as might have served to pass the time during the midnight watch on the bearded forecastle of Noah's ark. Was it that this old carpenter had been a lifelong wanderer, whose much rolling to and fro had not only gathered no moss but, what is more, had rubbed off whatever small outward attachments might originally have belonged to him? He was a stripped abstraction; an unbroken whole number; as uncompromised as a newborn baby; living without any deliberate reference to this world or the next. You might almost say that this strange uncompromisedness in him involved a sort of unintelligence; for in his numerous trades he did not seem to work so much by reason or by instinct, or simply because he had been taught to, or by any mixture of all these, even or uneven, but merely by a kind of deaf-and-dumb, spontaneous, literal process. He was a pure manipulator, a worker with the hands; his brain, if he had ever had one, must have oozed early on into the muscles of his fingers. He was like one of those unreasoning but still highly useful Sheffield contrivances, multum in parvo (much in little), which have the outside — though a little swollen — of a common pocketknife, but contain not only blades of various sizes but also screwdrivers, corkscrews, tweezers, awls, pens, rulers, nail-files, and countersinks. So if his superiors wanted to use the carpenter as a screwdriver, all they had to do was open that part of him, and the screw was fast; or if as tweezers, pick him up by the legs, and there they were.

Yet, as previously hinted, this all-tooled, open-and-shut carpenter was, after all, no mere machine or automaton. If he did not have a common soul in him, he had a subtle something that somehow did its duty in an odd way. What that was — whether an essence of quicksilver or a few drops of smelling salts — there is no telling. But there it was, and there it had resided for now some sixty years or more. And this it was, this same unaccountable, cunning life-principle in him, that kept him a great part of the time talking to himself; but only like an unreasoning wheel, which also hummingly talks to itself; or rather, his body was a sentry-box and this self-talker on guard there, and talking all the time to keep himself awake.
